title: White Matter & the Internal Capsule
summary: The wiring between regions: projection, association and commissural fibers.

lessons.title: Fiber Types: Projection, Association, Commissural

levels.kid:
Your brain has two kinds of stuff. The gray stuff is where brain cells think. The white stuff is wires that carry messages between them.

Why is it white? Each wire wears a fatty coat, like the plastic around a phone charger. The coat makes messages zoom fast.

There are three kinds of wires:

- Up-and-down wires go from the brain to the body, like an elevator.
- Neighbor wires connect parts on the same side, like a hallway.
- Bridge wires cross from the left side to the right side, like a bridge over a river.

When a wire breaks, two smart parts can't talk, even if both parts are fine.
levels.hs:
The brain is made of **gray matter** (neuron cell bodies, where processing happens) and **white matter** (bundles of axons, the cables that connect regions). White matter looks white because most axons are wrapped in **myelin**, a fatty insulating layer made by oligodendrocytes. Myelin lets signals jump between gaps called nodes of Ranvier, which makes them much faster.

White matter fibers are sorted into three families based on where they go:

- **Projection fibers** connect the cortex with lower structures: the thalamus, brainstem and spinal cord. The corticospinal tract, which carries movement commands to the spinal cord, is one example.
- **Association fibers** connect regions within the same hemisphere. Short ones (U-fibers) link neighboring gyri; long ones link distant lobes, like frontal to temporal.
- **Commissural fibers** cross the midline to link the two hemispheres. The biggest is the corpus callosum.

White matter makes up roughly half of the adult brain's volume. Damage to it, from a stroke, multiple sclerosis or trauma, can cause serious problems even when the cortex itself is untouched, because regions lose their connections. Doctors call this a disconnection.
levels.college:
White matter is organized into tracts named by their origin and termination, and classified into three systems.

**Projection fibers** run vertically between cortex and subcortical targets. Efferent projections include corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine and corticostriatal fibers; afferent projections are mainly thalamocortical radiations. Beneath the cortex they fan out as the **corona radiata**, then converge into the **internal capsule** between the thalamus/caudate medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally, and continue into the cerebral peduncles.

**Association fibers** stay within one hemisphere. **Short (arcuate or U-) fibers** loop just under the cortex between adjacent gyri. **Long association bundles** include the superior longitudinal fasciculus (with the arcuate fasciculus), the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, the uncinate fasciculus and the cingulum.

**Commissural fibers** connect homologous and heterotopic areas across the midline: the corpus callosum, the anterior commissure, the posterior commissure and the hippocampal commissure.

Myelination follows a predictable timetable: it begins prenatally, proceeds roughly caudal to rostral and posterior to anterior, and prefrontal association tracts keep maturing into the mid-20s. On T1 MRI in infants, myelinated white matter turns bright as myelin matures, which radiologists use to judge developmental age.

Clinically, white matter lesions produce deficits that depend on **which fibers pass through the lesion**, not on local cortical function. A small lesion in a dense crossroads like the internal capsule can cause a large deficit, while a similar-sized cortical lesion might be nearly silent. Diseases with a white matter preference include multiple sclerosis, small vessel ischemic disease, leukodystrophies, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and diffuse axonal injury.
levels.phd:
The projection/association/commissural taxonomy dates to 19th-century dissection (Meynert, Dejerine), and it remains useful, but modern work treats white matter as the physical substrate of a network, the **connectome**.

**Diffusion MRI** infers fiber orientation from the anisotropic diffusion of water along axons. The diffusion tensor yields fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean, axial and radial diffusivity. FA is not a direct measure of myelin: it falls with demyelination but also with axon loss, edema and, critically, **crossing fibers**. An estimated large majority of white matter voxels contain more than one fiber population, so tensor tractography produces both false negatives and false positives. Higher-order methods (constrained spherical deconvolution, multi-shell models, neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging) partially address this, but tractography still cannot determine axon direction or synapses.

Myelin is not just passive insulation. **Activity-dependent myelination** (oligodendrocyte precursors responding to neuronal firing) tunes conduction velocity and may synchronize arrival times across pathways of different lengths, a form of plasticity linked to motor learning in animal models. Oligodendrocytes also supply axons with lactate, which helps explain why demyelination leads to axonal degeneration.

White matter is vulnerable in distinctive ways. Deep white matter is supplied by long, thin medullary arterioles with few collaterals, making it a watershed for chronic hypoperfusion; this underlies small vessel disease and the leukoaraiosis seen in aging. Shearing forces in acceleration–deceleration trauma stretch axons at gray–white junctions, the corpus callosum and the dorsolateral brainstem, producing **diffuse axonal injury** with cytoskeletal disruption and delayed axotomy.

Current open questions include how much individual variation in tract anatomy matters functionally, and how far network models (hubs, rich-club organization) predict recovery after focal lesions. These are active research findings rather than settled clinical rules.
levels.expert:
For a neurosurgeon, white matter is where most permanent deficits are made. Cortex has some capacity for functional reorganization; major subcortical pathways have much less. A common teaching in glioma surgery is that the limits of a safe resection are often defined by **subcortical connectivity**, not by the cortical surface.

**Preoperative planning.** Diffusion tractography of the corticospinal tract, arcuate fasciculus and optic radiation is routinely fused into neuronavigation. Know its limits: tractography depends on seed choice and thresholds, underestimates fanning fibers (the lateral corticospinal fibers to face and hand are classically underrepresented), and is distorted by edema and tumor. Brain shift after dural opening and resection makes navigation drift, sometimes by a centimeter or more.

**Intraoperative confirmation.** Subcortical direct electrical stimulation remains the reference standard. Monopolar stimulation of the corticospinal tract evokes motor responses, and the stimulation threshold gives a rough estimate of distance to the tract; many teams slow down or stop as thresholds fall to low values. In awake surgery, stimulation of language bundles produces characteristic errors, which tells you which pathway you are on.

**Patterns on imaging.** Periventricular ovoid lesions perpendicular to the ventricles suggest demyelination; confluent periventricular hyperintensities in an older hypertensive patient suggest small vessel disease; lesions crossing the corpus callosum raise concern for glioblastoma or lymphoma. Microhemorrhages at the gray–white junction and corpus callosum on susceptibility-weighted imaging support diffuse axonal injury after trauma, even when CT looks unremarkable.

**Pitfall:** a patient with a dense deficit and a "small" lesion is not a mismatch. Always ask which fibers run through that spot. Localization in neurology is really localization of disconnected pathways as much as damaged gray matter.

keyPoints: Gray matter = cell bodies and processing; white matter = myelinated axon bundles.
Projection fibers link cortex with thalamus, brainstem and spinal cord (vertical).
Association fibers link regions within one hemisphere (short U-fibers and long bundles).
Commissural fibers cross the midline; the corpus callosum is the largest.
White matter lesions cause deficits by disconnection; small lesions in crowded tracts cause large deficits.
Diffusion tractography estimates tracts but struggles with crossing fibers.

examples.src: A patient with a tiny deep stroke has complete weakness of the opposite arm and leg, while the cortex looks normal.
examples.tr: The lesion hit a dense bundle of projection fibers, so a small spot cut many motor axons at once.

examples.src: An MRI shows ovoid lesions pointing away from the lateral ventricles in a young adult with prior vision loss.
examples.tr: Typical pattern of multiple sclerosis, a demyelinating white matter disease.

test.q: White matter looks white mainly because of:
test.explain: Myelin is lipid-rich and appears white; gray matter is mostly cell bodies and dendrites.

test.q: Fibers that connect the two hemispheres are called:
test.explain: Commissural fibers cross the midline, as in the corpus callosum.

test.q: The corticospinal tract is an example of which fiber type?
test.explain: It runs from cortex down to the spinal cord, so it is a projection tract.

test.q: Short association fibers linking neighboring gyri are called:
test.explain: They loop just beneath the cortex in a U shape between adjacent gyri.

test.q: Which cell makes myelin in the central nervous system?
test.explain: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves.

test.q: The fan of projection fibers just under the cortex, above the internal capsule, is the:
test.explain: Projection fibers fan out as the corona radiata and converge into the internal capsule.

test.q: Why can a very small internal capsule stroke cause a large deficit?
choices: It contains the primary motor cortex
The internal capsule is gray matter
It controls blood flow to the cortex
Many tightly packed fibers pass through a small space
test.explain: The capsule is a crowded crossroads of projection fibers, so a small lesion cuts many axons.

test.q: Which disease primarily targets myelin in the central nervous system?
test.explain: MS is an immune-mediated demyelinating disease with white matter plaques.

test.q: A known weakness of diffusion tensor tractography is:
test.explain: A single tensor per voxel cannot represent several fiber directions, causing false tracts and missed ones.

test.q: Fibers that stay within one hemisphere are called ___ fibers.
test.explain: Association fibers connect regions within the same hemisphere.

test.q: Name the largest commissure of the brain (2 words).
test.explain: The corpus callosum carries hundreds of millions of axons between the hemispheres.

test.q: Gaps in myelin where the signal jumps are called nodes of ___.
test.explain: Saltatory conduction jumps from node of Ranvier to node, speeding signals.

test.q: Name the injury from shearing forces that damages axons at the gray–white junction and corpus callosum (3 words).
test.explain: Acceleration–deceleration trauma stretches axons, causing diffuse axonal injury.

kidTest.q: What do white matter wires do?
kidTest.explain: White matter is the brain's wiring.

kidTest.q: Why are the wires white?
kidTest.explain: The fatty coat is called myelin.

kidTest.q: Wires that cross from left side to right side are like a:
kidTest.explain: Bridge wires connect the two halves of the brain.

kidTest.q: The fatty coat makes messages go:
kidTest.explain: Insulation helps signals zoom.

kidTest.q: What color is the thinking stuff of the brain?
kidTest.explain: Gray matter is where brain cells do their thinking.

kidTest.q: If a wire breaks, what happens?
choices: Two brain parts can't talk well
kidTest.explain: Broken wires mean lost connections.

advancedTest.q: Fractional anisotropy falls in a white matter region. The most defensible interpretation is:
choices: Microstructure changed, but FA alone cannot say whether myelin, axons or fiber geometry caused it
advancedTest.explain: FA is sensitive but not specific: edema, axon loss, demyelination and crossing fibers all lower it.

advancedTest.q: Why is deep periventricular white matter vulnerable to chronic hypoperfusion?
choices: It is fed by long, thin medullary arterioles with few collaterals
It has no blood supply at all
It is drained by the cavernous sinus
It receives blood only from the external carotid
advancedTest.explain: Long penetrating arterioles make deep white matter a watershed, underlying small vessel disease.

advancedTest.q: During glioma resection, subcortical motor stimulation thresholds are falling steadily. The best interpretation is:
choices: The resection is getting closer to the corticospinal tract
advancedTest.explain: Lower thresholds roughly mean shorter distance to the tract, a signal to slow or stop.

advancedTest.q: Why do demyelinated axons tend to degenerate over time?
choices: Loss of oligodendrocyte trophic and metabolic support, plus energy failure from redistributed sodium channels
advancedTest.explain: Oligodendrocytes supply axons metabolically; denuded axons face higher energy demands and degenerate.

lessons.title: The Internal Capsule

levels.kid:
Deep inside your brain there is a super busy hallway called the internal capsule. Almost every message going from your brain down to your body squeezes through it.

It is shaped like a boomerang, with a front part, a bend and a back part.

The back part carries the "move!" messages to your arms and legs. It also carries "I feel that!" messages coming up from your body.

Because so many wires squeeze into this small hallway, even a tiny blockage can make one whole side of the body weak. It's like one fallen tree blocking a busy road.
levels.hs:
The **internal capsule** is a thick band of white matter deep in each hemisphere. It sits between the thalamus and caudate nucleus on the inside and the lentiform nucleus (putamen plus globus pallidus) on the outside. Almost all fibers traveling between the cortex and the brainstem or spinal cord pass through it.

Seen in a horizontal (axial) slice, it looks like a sideways V or boomerang with three parts:

- **Anterior limb**: between the caudate head and the lentiform nucleus. Carries fibers connecting the frontal lobe with the thalamus and pons.
- **Genu** (the bend): classically carries corticobulbar fibers that control face and throat muscles.
- **Posterior limb**: between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus. Carries the corticospinal tract to the arm and leg, and sensory fibers from the thalamus to the sensory cortex.

Behind and below the lentiform nucleus run the visual and hearing radiations.

The capsule is fed by tiny deep arteries, mostly the **lenticulostriate arteries** from the middle cerebral artery. High blood pressure damages these small vessels. A blockage causes a **lacunar stroke**; a classic result is pure motor weakness of the face, arm and leg on the opposite side, with no numbness or language problem.
levels.college:
On axial sections the internal capsule has five parts.

- **Anterior limb** (caudate head medially, lentiform laterally): anterior thalamic radiation linking mediodorsal and anterior thalamic nuclei with prefrontal and cingulate cortex, plus frontopontine fibers.
- **Genu**: corticobulbar fibers to cranial nerve motor nuclei (classically placed here, though tract studies show them more spread out).
- **Posterior limb** (thalamus medially, lentiform laterally): corticospinal fibers, with a rough somatotopy (arm fibers anterior to leg fibers), plus thalamocortical fibers from VPL and VPM to the postcentral gyrus. Corticospinal fibers lie mostly in the posterior half of the posterior limb.
- **Retrolenticular part**: optic radiation from the lateral geniculate nucleus.
- **Sublenticular part**: auditory radiation from the medial geniculate nucleus to Heschl's gyrus, and the anterior loop of the optic radiation (Meyer's loop).

**Blood supply**: lenticulostriate branches of the MCA supply most of the upper capsule; the **anterior choroidal artery** supplies the lower posterior limb and retrolenticular part; the recurrent artery of Heubner (from the ACA) and medial lenticulostriates supply the anterior limb and head of caudate.

**Lacunar syndromes** come from occlusion of single penetrating arteries, usually from lipohyalinosis due to chronic hypertension or diabetes. Pure motor hemiparesis localizes to the posterior limb (or basis pontis); ataxic hemiparesis and dysarthria–clumsy hand can arise in the capsule or pons. Lacunes are under 15 mm and spare cortical signs such as aphasia, neglect and visual field cuts.

The putamen, right next to the capsule, is the most common site of **hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage**; the resulting hemiplegia is due to capsular compression and destruction.
levels.phd:
The classical capsular map comes from lesion correlation and fiber dissection, and it has been refined by diffusion tractography and stimulation.

**Somatotopy is dynamic along the course.** In the corona radiata, corticospinal fibers are arranged roughly by cortical origin. As they descend into the posterior limb they rotate and compact, so face, arm and leg fibers become ordered from anterior to posterior within the posterior third of the limb. Older diagrams placing the corticospinal tract in the anterior posterior limb, near the genu, were revised by studies combining tractography with stroke outcome. This matters for predicting recovery: a lesion load on the corticospinal tract within the posterior limb is a stronger predictor of motor outcome than total infarct volume.

**The anterior limb is a frontothalamic and frontostriatal highway.** It carries reciprocal prefrontal–thalamic fibers (especially mediodorsal) and corticostriatal and corticopontine fibers, with a medial-to-lateral and dorsal-to-ventral organization that tractography studies relate to orbitofrontal, ventromedial and dorsolateral prefrontal regions. This is the anatomical basis for **ventral capsule/ventral striatum** neuromodulation in severe, treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder and investigational use in depression, where outcome has been linked to which specific fiber bundle is engaged rather than to a gray-matter target.

**Wallerian degeneration** after a capsular infarct can be followed on MRI down through the cerebral peduncle and pons over weeks to months, an imaging biomarker of tract damage.

**Capsular warning syndrome** describes repeated, stereotyped transient episodes of lacunar-type weakness over hours to days, with a high risk of subsequent infarction. Its mechanism (hemodynamic failure in a single diseased penetrating artery versus other causes) is debated, and optimal acute management is not settled.
levels.expert:
**Deep brain stimulation.** The internal capsule is the most common source of stimulation side effects. With STN or GPi leads, current spreading into the posterior limb produces tonic muscle contraction of the contralateral face or hand, or dysarthria, at a characteristic threshold. Programming nurses and neurologists use these capsular thresholds as landmarks; intraoperatively, macrostimulation to find capsular responses tells you the lead is too lateral (for STN) or too posterior/medial (for GPi). For essential tremor, a VIM lead that is too anterior and lateral likewise stimulates the capsule.

**Intracerebral hemorrhage.** Putaminal hemorrhage destroys or compresses the posterior limb. Surgical evacuation of supratentorial ICH remains debated: large trials of open craniotomy were broadly neutral, catheter evacuation with thrombolytic irrigation did not improve the primary outcome, and a recent trial of minimally invasive parafascicular evacuation showed benefit driven mainly by lobar hemorrhages. Know the current guideline language and its uncertainty rather than quoting one trial.

**Approaches near the capsule.** Transsylvian approaches to the insula must respect the lateral lenticulostriate arteries, which define the medial limit of insular glioma resection; injuring them causes a capsular infarct and hemiplegia despite a perfect cortical resection. Transcortical routes to the lateral ventricle and thalamus must also avoid the posterior limb. Anterior choroidal artery injury during aneurysm clipping at the ICA can cause the triad of contralateral hemiparesis, hemisensory loss and homonymous hemianopia.

**Imaging pearl:** acute posterior limb infarcts can be tiny on CT; diffusion-weighted MRI is far more sensitive. When you see a pure motor syndrome with a normal CT, think lacune and get an MRI. Pure sensory stroke points instead to the thalamus (VPL/VPM).

**Ablative psychiatric surgery** such as anterior capsulotomy is now performed in a few centers with radiosurgery, radiofrequency or focused ultrasound under strict ethics review.

keyPoints: The internal capsule lies between thalamus/caudate (medial) and lentiform nucleus (lateral).
Anterior limb: frontal–thalamic and frontopontine fibers.
Genu: corticobulbar fibers (classic teaching).
Posterior limb: corticospinal and thalamocortical somatosensory fibers.
Retrolenticular/sublenticular parts: optic and auditory radiations.
Lenticulostriate arteries (MCA) and anterior choroidal artery supply it; lacunar strokes cause pure motor hemiparesis.

examples.src: A 68-year-old with long-standing high blood pressure wakes with weakness of the left face, arm and leg, no numbness, no speech or vision problems.
examples.tr: Pure motor lacunar stroke in the right posterior limb of the internal capsule (or basis pontis).

examples.src: During DBS programming, raising the voltage makes the patient's opposite hand pull into a sustained contraction.
examples.tr: Current is spreading into corticospinal fibers of the internal capsule.

Lesion load on the corticospinal tract within the posterior limb

In the red nucleus causing tremor

advancedTest.explain: Injury to the lenticulostriates causes capsular infarction and hemiplegia.

advancedTest.explain: Response appears linked to which anterior limb bundle is engaged.

lessons.title: Corpus Callosum & Commissures

levels.kid:
Your brain has a left half and a right half. They need to talk all the time, so they are joined by a big bridge called the corpus callosum. It is made of millions and millions of tiny wires.

The left half mostly controls the right side of your body, and the right half controls the left side. The bridge helps them share what each one knows.

There are a few smaller bridges too, like little side roads.

Long ago, some doctors cut part of this bridge to stop very bad seizures from spreading from one half to the other. It helped those people a lot.
levels.hs:
The two cerebral hemispheres are connected by **commissures**, bundles of axons that cross the midline. The largest by far is the **corpus callosum**, an arched band of roughly 200 million axons (estimates vary) lying at the bottom of the deep groove between the hemispheres.

From front to back, the corpus callosum has a **rostrum**, a **genu** (the front bend), a **body** and a thick back end called the **splenium**. Front fibers connect the frontal lobes; splenium fibers connect the occipital and parts of the temporal and parietal lobes, including the visual areas.

Smaller commissures include:

- the **anterior commissure**, linking parts of the temporal lobes and olfactory areas
- the **posterior commissure**, involved in the pupillary light reflex and vertical eye movements
- the **hippocampal commissure**, linking the two hippocampi through the fornix

In the 1960s, Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga studied "split-brain" patients whose corpus callosum had been cut to treat severe epilepsy. When an object was shown only to the right hemisphere, many patients could not name it out loud, because speech is usually in the left hemisphere, yet their left hand could pick it out. Sperry won a Nobel Prize in 1981 partly for this work.
levels.college:
**Corpus callosum anatomy.** Segments (anterior to posterior): rostrum, genu, body (trunk), isthmus and splenium. Callosal fibers are largely homotopic (connecting mirror-image areas) with some heterotopic projections. Genu fibers form the forceps minor to the frontal lobes; splenium fibers form the forceps major to the occipital lobes. Primary sensory and motor hand areas have relatively sparse callosal connections compared with association cortex.

**Blood supply.** Most of the corpus callosum is supplied by the pericallosal artery (ACA); the splenium receives posterior pericallosal branches from the PCA. Because of this rich, dual supply, isolated callosal infarcts are uncommon.

**Other commissures.** The anterior commissure crosses in the lamina terminalis, connecting the anterior temporal lobes and olfactory structures. The posterior commissure lies at the junction of the midbrain and third ventricle; its fibers serve the pupillary light reflex (pretectal nuclei) and vertical gaze, so lesions here cause Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome features. The hippocampal commissure links the crura of the fornix. The habenular commissure lies above the pineal recess.

**Disconnection after callosal section.** With the left hemisphere dominant for language: inability to name objects felt with the left hand (left tactile anomia), left-hand apraxia to verbal command, left-hand agraphia, and inability to read words flashed to the left visual field. Most patients appear normal in daily life.

**Agenesis of the corpus callosum** is one of the more common brain malformations. On imaging the lateral ventricles are parallel and widely separated, with enlarged occipital horns (colpocephaly), and the third ventricle may rise between them. Many uncrossed fibers run front-to-back as **Probst bundles**. Outcome ranges from normal to severe disability, depending on associated anomalies.

Lesions crossing the corpus callosum ("butterfly" pattern) suggest glioblastoma or primary CNS lymphoma.
levels.phd:
The corpus callosum is the largest fiber system in the brain and a model system for interhemispheric communication.

**Function is both excitatory and inhibitory.** Callosal axons are mostly glutamatergic, but they synapse on inhibitory interneurons as well as pyramidal cells, so the net effect can be **interhemispheric inhibition**. Transcranial magnetic stimulation shows that activating one motor cortex briefly suppresses the other. This underpins the "interhemispheric competition" model of stroke recovery, where the undamaged hemisphere may suppress the damaged one. Trials of inhibiting the healthy hemisphere with non-invasive stimulation have given mixed results, and the model is now considered too simple; the healthy hemisphere can also support recovery, especially after large lesions.

**Fiber composition varies by segment.** Histology shows thin, slowly conducting fibers concentrated in the genu (prefrontal connections) and larger, faster fibers in the posterior body and splenium (sensorimotor and visual). Interhemispheric transfer time is on the order of milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, measured behaviorally with the Poffenberger paradigm.

**Split-brain research continues to be debated.** Classic studies described two semi-independent streams of consciousness. Later work in a small number of patients suggested unified awareness with divided perception, and that some information may cross through subcortical pathways. Generalizing from a few patients, often with longstanding epilepsy and possible reorganization, is a recognized limitation.

**Development.** Callosal axons cross via guidance by midline glial structures (the glial wedge, indusium griseum glia, midline zipper glia) and molecules such as netrin, Slit/Robo and DCC. Mutations in these pathways are linked to callosal agenesis, sometimes with mirror movements. Sex and handedness differences in callosal size were once widely claimed; many have not held up after correcting for brain size.
levels.expert:
**Corpus callosotomy** is a palliative epilepsy operation for drop attacks (atonic or tonic seizures) that cause falls and injuries, often in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome. It disrupts seizure spread rather than removing a focus. Many surgeons first section the anterior two-thirds, which often controls drop attacks with less disconnection; a completion to the splenium is done if needed. Endoscopic and laser ablation techniques are increasingly used. Vagus nerve stimulation is the usual alternative, and the choice depends on seizure type and local practice.

**The interhemispheric transcallosal approach** reaches the lateral and third ventricles: colloid cysts, intraventricular tumors and some thalamic lesions. Key points: a bridging-vein-sparing craniotomy over the coronal suture (bridging veins enter the superior sagittal sinus and sacrificing them risks venous infarction); retraction of the medial frontal lobe; identifying the paired pericallosal arteries (not the callosomarginals) before opening the callosum; and a short callosotomy, typically about 2 cm, in the body. Small anterior callosal openings rarely cause clinical disconnection, but posterior extension into the splenium risks it, especially combined with other lesions.

**Imaging patterns to recognize:**

- **Butterfly lesions** crossing the genu or splenium: glioblastoma or lymphoma; biopsy before resection when lymphoma is a possibility, because steroids can make it melt away and hide the diagnosis.
- **Diffuse axonal injury**: callosal microhemorrhages, especially at the splenium, are part of standard grading.
- **Cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum**: a small, oval, diffusion-restricting splenial lesion seen with seizures, infections, metabolic disturbance or medication changes, usually reversible. Do not mistake it for infarct or tumor.
- **Demyelination**: lesions at the callosal–septal interface on sagittal FLAIR are a strong clue for MS.

**Alien hand phenomena** can follow callosal injury (the left hand acting at cross purposes with the right) and should be explained to families before callosal surgery.

keyPoints: Commissures connect the two hemispheres; the corpus callosum is the largest.
Corpus callosum parts: rostrum, genu, body, isthmus, splenium.
Anterior commissure links temporal and olfactory areas; posterior commissure serves the pupillary reflex and vertical gaze.
Split-brain patients cannot name objects felt by the left hand (with left-hemisphere language).
Callosotomy treats drop attacks; anterior two-thirds is often done first.
Lesions crossing the corpus callosum suggest glioblastoma or lymphoma.

examples.src: After callosotomy, a patient holds a key in the left hand behind a screen and cannot name it, but can pick it from a tray with the left hand.

lessons.title: Association Bundles & Disconnection Syndromes

levels.kid:
Inside each half of your brain there are long wire cables that connect faraway parts, like phone lines between towns.

One cable connects the "hearing words" part to the "saying words" part. If that cable breaks, a person can understand you and talk, but they can't repeat what you just said. Funny, right?

Another cable connects the seeing part to the part that knows faces and things.

When a cable breaks but both towns are fine, doctors call it a disconnection. The towns still work, they just can't send messages to each other.
levels.hs:
**Association bundles** are long white matter cables that connect distant regions within the same hemisphere. Some important ones:

- **Arcuate fasciculus** (part of the superior longitudinal fasciculus): arches around the Sylvian fissure, linking language areas in the temporal lobe (Wernicke's area) with the frontal lobe (Broca's area).
- **Inferior longitudinal fasciculus**: runs from the occipital lobe to the temporal lobe; helps with recognizing objects and faces.
- **Uncinate fasciculus**: a hook-shaped bundle linking the frontal lobe's underside with the front of the temporal lobe; involved in emotion and memory.
- **Cingulum**: runs inside the cingulate gyrus, part of the limbic system.

A **disconnection syndrome** happens when the regions are healthy but the cable between them is cut. In the 1960s, neurologist Norman Geschwind made this idea famous.

Classic example: **conduction aphasia**. Damage to the arcuate fasciculus region leaves a person able to understand speech and talk fluently, but they struggle to repeat sentences and make sound errors, like saying "spoot" for "spoon."

Another example: **alexia without agraphia**. A stroke in the left occipital lobe and the back of the corpus callosum leaves someone able to write but unable to read, even what they just wrote, because visual information can't reach the language areas.
levels.college:
**Major long association tracts:**

- **Superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF)**: frontoparietal system, often divided into SLF I–III, important for attention, spatial awareness and motor planning. Right-sided SLF damage contributes to neglect.
- **Arcuate fasciculus (AF)**: perisylvian arching fibers linking posterior temporal cortex with inferior frontal and precentral cortex; dorsal stream for mapping sound to articulation.
- **Inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF)**: from occipital and posterior temporal cortex through the temporal stem and external/extreme capsule to the frontal lobe; implicated in semantic processing (ventral stream).
- **Inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF)**: occipitotemporal; visual recognition and reading.
- **Uncinate fasciculus (UF)**: orbitofrontal to anterior temporal pole through the temporal stem; emotion, semantic memory for names.
- **Cingulum**: cingulate to parahippocampal gyrus; limbic and memory functions.

**Geschwind's disconnection framework (1965):** higher functions can be lost by severing connections between intact regions.

- **Conduction aphasia**: fluent speech with phonemic paraphasias, good comprehension, disproportionately poor repetition. Classically AF; often involves the supramarginal gyrus and underlying white matter.
- **Alexia without agraphia** (Dejerine 1892): left PCA infarct damaging left occipital cortex and the splenium. Right homonymous hemianopia; the intact right occipital cortex sees words but can't send them across to the left angular gyrus. Writing is preserved.
- **Ideomotor apraxia**: inability to perform learned gestures on command despite intact strength and comprehension; may reflect disconnection of left parietal praxis representations from motor areas.
- **Callosal disconnection**: left-hand apraxia, agraphia and tactile anomia.

Recognizing disconnection syndromes is a localization skill: the deficit points to the pathway, and the pathway points to the lesion.
levels.phd:
**From classical connectionism to hodotopy.** The 19th-century Wernicke–Lichtheim model (centers connected by pathways) was revived by Geschwind. Later work showed its limits: conduction aphasia can result from cortical damage to the supramarginal gyrus and posterior superior temporal cortex without AF injury, and pure AF lesions do not always cause it. The modern **dual-stream model** (Hickok and Poeppel) proposes a dorsal stream (AF/SLF) mapping sound to articulation and a ventral stream (IFOF, ILF, UF, middle longitudinal fasciculus) mapping sound to meaning. Duffau's **hodotopic** view emphasizes that function emerges from parallel, partially redundant subnetworks: cortex (topology) plus connections (hodology).

**Evidence from intraoperative stimulation.** During awake surgery, stimulating the AF/SLF tends to produce **phonemic paraphasias** and repetition errors, while stimulating the IFOF produces **semantic paraphasias** (saying "cat" for "dog"). This double dissociation, accumulated over large series, is among the strongest causal evidence about human white matter function, though it is limited to patients with lesions and possible reorganization.

**Tract controversies.** The very existence of the IFOF as a direct fronto-occipital connection was debated for decades, because it is clear in human dissection and tractography but hard to demonstrate with tracer methods in monkeys. The extent of the AF, its relation to SLF III, and leftward asymmetry are also argued. Tractography reproducibility depends heavily on processing choices; a 2017 international challenge showed many algorithms produced numerous false-positive bundles.

**Network neurology.** Lesion network mapping uses large normative connectomes to ask which network a lesion disrupts, finding that lesions in different locations causing the same symptom often share a connected network. This approach is promising but depends on normative data and remains a research tool.
levels.expert:
**Awake language mapping** is where association bundles become operational. A typical left dominant glioma resection: identify cortical language sites with direct stimulation (counting, picture naming, sometimes reading or semantic association tasks), then resect, repeatedly stimulating the cavity walls. Many centers resect up to functional boundaries rather than with a fixed safety margin from positive sites.

Error type points to the bundle:

- **Phonemic paraphasias / repetition errors**: dorsal stream, AF/SLF (deep to the supramarginal gyrus and posterior frontal operculum).
- **Semantic paraphasias**: IFOF, often deep in the temporal stem or the floor of an insular or frontal resection.
- **Anomia without paraphasia** at the temporal pole region: can involve uncinate/ILF connections, though these are often considered more compensable.
- **Speech arrest**: ventral premotor cortex or the frontal aslant tract, which links supplementary motor area with the inferior frontal gyrus. Frontal aslant injury contributes to transient speech initiation problems after SMA-region resections.

**Supplementary motor area syndrome**: after resection of the SMA, patients can have contralateral akinesia and mutism that look catastrophic in the first days but usually recover over weeks. Counsel families beforehand; it is not the same as corticospinal injury.

**Visual pathways.** Temporal lobe surgery (anterior temporal lobectomy or approaches through the temporal stem) can cut Meyer's loop, causing a contralateral superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"). Tractography of the optic radiation is used to plan trajectories, including laser ablation for mesial temporal epilepsy.

**Neglect** after right-sided surgery correlates with SLF II/III injury; testing line bisection intraoperatively has been used in awake right parietal cases.

**Bedside localization**: fluent speech, good comprehension, poor repetition = think conduction aphasia, dominant supramarginal region. Can write but cannot read, with right hemianopia = left PCA territory including splenium.

keyPoints: Association bundles link distant regions within one hemisphere.
Arcuate fasciculus links temporal (Wernicke) and frontal (Broca) language areas.
IFOF, ILF and uncinate form ventral pathways; SLF/AF form the dorsal pathway.
Conduction aphasia: fluent, good comprehension, poor repetition, phonemic errors.
Alexia without agraphia: left PCA stroke hitting left occipital cortex and splenium.
In awake surgery, AF stimulation gives phonemic errors; IFOF stimulation gives semantic errors.

examples.src: A patient speaks fluently and follows commands, but when asked to repeat "no ifs, ands or buts" says "no its, ants or bups."
